This vignette covers probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA), including
parameter sampling, the cost-effectiveness plane, the cost-effectiveness
acceptability curve (CEAC), and expected loss curves.

## Why PSA?

Deterministic sensitivity analysis varies one parameter at a time, but real
uncertainty is joint --- multiple parameters are uncertain simultaneously.
PSA propagates this joint uncertainty through the model by sampling all
parameters from their distributions and re-running the model thousands of
times (Claxton et al., 2005; Briggs et al., 2006).

Each PSA iteration produces a cost-QALY pair per strategy. The collection of
iterations maps out the joint distribution of incremental costs and effects.

## Parameter Distributions

ShinyCEA supports 7 distributions for PSA sampling. The choice depends on the
parameter's domain and the available evidence:

| Distribution | Domain | Typical use | Parameterized from |
|:------------|:-------|:-----------|:-------------------|
| Beta | [0, 1] | Probabilities, utilities | Mean + 95% CI |
| Gamma | [0, Inf) | Costs | Mean + 95% CI |
| Log-normal | (0, Inf) | Hazard ratios, relative risks | Mean + 95% CI |
| Normal | (-Inf, Inf) | Treatment effects (unbounded) | Mean + 95% CI |
| Uniform | [a, b] | Ranges with no central tendency | Lower, upper |
| Triangular | [a, b] | Expert elicitation (mode + bounds) | Lower, mode, upper |
| PERT | [a, b] | Smoother than triangular | Lower, mode, upper |

The `mean`, `lower`, and `upper` columns in the parameter table define the
distribution. ShinyCEA uses method-of-moments matching to derive the shape
parameters internally --- you don't need to specify alpha/beta or shape/rate
directly (Briggs et al., 2006, Ch. 4).

## Running PSA

```{r psa}
library(ShinyCEA)
m <- cea_sick_sicker()
set.seed(20250605)
psa <- run_psa(m, m$default_params(), n_sim = 1000)
cat("Iterations used:", psa$used, "| Dropped:", psa$dropped)
```

Dropped iterations are those where the model returned non-finite values for
at least one strategy. A high drop rate indicates parameter ranges that
produce impossible model states.

## Cost-Effectiveness Plane

The CE plane plots incremental costs ($\Delta C$) against incremental QALYs
($\Delta E$) for each PSA iteration, relative to the reference strategy.
The WTP threshold appears as a diagonal line --- points below it are
cost-effective (Fenwick et al., 2004).

```{r ce-plane}
det <- run_deterministic(m, m$default_params(), wtp = 100000)
ref <- det$ref

inc_list <- lapply(setdiff(m$info()$strategies, ref), function(s) {
  data.frame(
    strategy = s,
    inc_qaly = psa$results[[paste0(s, ".q")]] - psa$results[[paste0(ref, ".q")]],
    inc_cost = psa$results[[paste0(s, ".cost")]] - psa$results[[paste0(ref, ".cost")]]
  )
})
inc_df <- do.call(rbind, inc_list)
plot_ce_plane(inc_df, wtp = 100000)
```

Points in the **southeast quadrant** (more effective, less costly) represent
iterations where the intervention dominates. Points in the **northwest**
quadrant represent iterations where the intervention is dominated.

## PSA Summary Table

```{r psa-summary}
summ <- build_psa_summary(psa$results, m$info()$strategies, wtp = 100000)
summ
```

Each cell shows the mean with 95% credible interval from the PSA iterations.

## Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)

The CEAC shows, for each WTP threshold, the probability that each strategy
has the highest NMB. It synthesizes the full PSA into a decision-relevant
summary (Fenwick et al., 2004; Lothgren & Zethraeus, 2000).

```{r ceac}
ceac <- compute_ceac(psa$results, m$info()$strategies,
                     wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 2000)
plot_ceac(ceac)
```

At low WTP, the cheapest strategy tends to be optimal. As WTP increases,
more effective (and costly) strategies become preferred. The crossing points
indicate where the optimal strategy switches.

**Limitation of CEAC:** The probability of being cost-effective does not
account for the *magnitude* of the loss from choosing the wrong strategy.
A strategy can have a 51% probability of being optimal while the expected
loss from choosing it is large. The expected loss curve addresses this.

## Expected Loss

Expected loss (also called expected opportunity loss) measures, for each
strategy at each WTP, the average monetary loss compared to perfect
information. The optimal strategy is the one that **minimizes expected
loss**, which is equivalent to maximizing expected NMB but also conveys the
magnitude of decision uncertainty (Alarid-Escudero et al., 2019).

$$\text{EL}_s(\lambda) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ \max_j \text{NMB}_{ij}(\lambda) - \text{NMB}_{is}(\lambda) \right]$$

The minimum expected loss across strategies equals the EVPI.

```{r expected-loss}
el <- compute_expected_loss(psa$results, m$info()$strategies,
                            wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 2000)
plot_expected_loss(el)
```

Compared to the CEAC:

- CEAC shows the *probability* of being optimal (binary: best or not).
- Expected loss shows the *magnitude* of the wrong decision (continuous: how much you lose).

When two strategies have similar probability of being optimal (~50/50), the
expected loss reveals which one has a smaller penalty when it's wrong.

## PSA Parameter Draws

Inspecting the distributions of parameter draws helps verify that the
sampling is working as intended:

```{r draws}
head(psa$draws[, 1:5], 5)
```

- Briggs, A. H., Claxton, K., & Sculpher, M. J. (2006). *Decision Modelling
